desc:
In one operation you add 1 to or subtract 1 from any element of nums. Elements may become negative or exceed the original range.

Return the minimum number of operations needed to make nums non-decreasing (nums[i] ≤ nums[i+1] for all valid i).

[3, 1, 2]       -> 2   ([2, 2, 2] or [1, 1, 2])
[5, 4, 3, 2, 1] -> 6   ([3, 3, 3, 3, 3])
[1, 2, 3]       -> 0
hints: Raising only or lowering only is not always best. Think about what the final array looks like and how it relates to the original values.
A good final array only uses values that already occur in nums, and a simple left-to-right greedy with a heap can find the cost without trying all of them.

Keep a max-heap of the values seen so far. For each x push x. If the heap top is larger than x, the prefix is out of order: add top - x to the answer, pop the top and push x again. The total at the end is the minimum cost.
editorial: Sweep from left to right and keep a max-heap that stores, implicitly, the best non-decreasing 'target' values for the prefix. When the new value x is at least the largest stored value, the prefix stays sorted for free. Otherwise some earlier target has to come down to meet x or x has to go up; either way the cheapest fix costs top - x operations.

Concretely: push x; if heap.top > x, add heap.top - x to the cost, remove the top and push x a second time. The second push of x records that the removed target and the new element now share the level x. This is the 'slope trick' for L1 isotonic regression: the heap top is always the cheapest level that the current prefix can be lowered to.
Each element causes O(1) heap operations, so the time is O(n log n) and the space is O(n). The answer is at most about 5 * 10<sup>8</sup> for these limits, so it fits in 32 bits.
